Number one. Your old account doesn't get the old deal anymore.

I know. You opened that account forty years ago, and it was free. Free checking. Maybe they even gave you a toaster. Here's what actually happens. Banks retire old account types all the time. When they do, they move your account into a new product, and they send you a letter. One letter. It says something like "important changes to your account agreement." And in that new agreement there's a monthly maintenance fee, and the only way to avoid it is to keep a minimum balance, or have a direct deposit, or sign up for paper-free statements.

So here's what you do. Look at your last three statements, line by line, and look for the words "maintenance fee" or "service charge." If you see one, call or go in and ask one question: "Which account do you have today with no monthly fee that I qualify for?" Most banks still have one. Many have a senior account. They just don't move you there on their own. You have to ask. Old account, new rules. Read the letter.
Number two. Taking out your own cash now comes with questions, you see?

You walk in to withdraw a few thousand dollars, and the teller asks what it's for, or calls a manager, or asks you to wait. You feel like a suspect. Here's what actually happens behind that counter. Banks are required to file a report with the government when someone takes out more than ten thousand dollars in cash in one day. That's the law, and it's not about you. But on top of that, tellers are trained to watch for one thing with older customers: scams. Somebody on the phone telling grandma to take out cash and not tell anybody. It happens every single week, friend. I saw it. Grown children in tears in my office.

So when the teller asks, she's not being nosy. She's following a script designed to catch the scammer who might be standing behind you. Here's how you make it painless. If you need a large amount, call the branch a day ahead. Big cash withdrawals often need to be ordered anyway, because the branch doesn't keep that much in the drawer. And one more thing, and please hear me: never, ever break a big withdrawal into smaller pieces to avoid the report. That has a name, it's called structuring, and that is illegal even when the money is completely clean. Just take it out and let them file the paper. The paper doesn't hurt you. Hiding from it does.
Number three. The bank can now hold your transaction if they think you're being exploited.

This one surprises people. Banks today... Banks today are allowed, and encouraged, to delay a transaction when they suspect an older customer is being taken advantage of. A big wire to someone you met online, okay? A sudden transfer to a new "investment advisor." A grandson nobody has seen in ten years who suddenly needs bail money.

I'm going to be honest with you: this rule saved more of my customers than anything else in thirty-five years. But it also means one day a transfer you really wanted to make might get stopped, and you'll be annoyed. So here's the fix, and it's simple. Ask your bank to add a trusted contact person to your account. It's a form. It doesn't give that person any access to your money. None. It only means that if the bank is worried, they can call your daughter or your nephew or your friend from church before they do anything. One form. It protects you from the scammer and it protects you from the bank guessing wrong.
Number four. This is the one my sister got angry about. Now, Your joint account might not do what you think.

A lot... A lot of folks, when they get older, add a son or a daughter to their checking account. "So they can help me pay the bills." Here's what actually happens. On most joint accounts, that person now legally owns that money as much as you do. Uh... They can take it out. Their creditors can sometimes go after it. If they get divorced, it can get dragged into it. And when you pass away, that money goes straight to them, not to your will. So if you have three kids and you added one, the other two might get nothing from that account, even if your will says split it three ways. I watched families stop speaking to each other over this, in my lobby.

If you only want help paying bills, ask about adding an authorized signer or a convenience signer instead, where your bank offers it, or give someone a financial power of attorney. Well, And if you want the money to go to specific people when you die, ask for a payable-on-death beneficiary on the account. That's a simple form. The money skips probate and goes exactly where you said. Help with the bills and ownership of the money are two different things. Don't mix them.
Number five. The bank might not accept your power of attorney.

You did everything right. You went to a lawyer, you signed a power of attorney so your daughter can handle things if you get sick. And then your daughter walks into the bank with it, and they say no. "We need our own form." Or "this is too old." Or "we have to send it to legal," and that takes three weeks.

Here's what actually happens. Banks are... Banks are nervous about powers of attorney because they've been used for fraud. So many banks have their own form, and they like that one better. Some states have rules that make banks accept a properly signed power of attorney, but even then there are delays. So here's what you do, while you're healthy, this month: take your power of attorney into your branch, with the person you named, and ask them to review it and put it on file now. Ask them, straight out: "If I get sick tomorrow, will you accept this?" If they say they need their own form, fill out their form too. Do it while you can still walk in and sign. Number six. Paper is starting to cost you.

Paper statements. Paper checks. Talking to a human being, okay? Little by little, these things got fees attached. A charge for a paper statement. A charge for a teller-assisted transfer that would be free online. A charge for a cashier's check.

Here's the thing. Now, Banks want you online because a branch is expensive. I understand that. But you shouldn't be paying a penalty for liking paper. So look for the fees, and ask. Many banks waive paper statement fees for customers over a certain age, or for certain accounts. You only find out if you ask. Number seven. Now, Your certificate of deposit renewed itself at a worse rate.

You opened a CD at a good rate. It matured. And you didn't notice, because there was a short window, usually seven to ten days, and the bank sent one notice. So it... So it rolled over automatically, often into a new CD at whatever the standard rate was that day, which may be much lower than the special rate they were advertising to new customers that same week.

Here's what you do. Write the maturity date of every CD on your calendar, in red, and put a second note one week before it. When it matures, call and ask: "What's your best rate right now, including promotional rates?" If they won't match, you're allowed to take that money somewhere else. That's the whole trick. Your loyalty is not paying you interest. The calendar is.
Number eight. The branch you counted on might close.

Well, I have to tell you this one, because I lived it. Banks have closed thousands of branches over the last years. Mine was almost one of them. Know where your second-nearest branch is. Uh... Know your bank's phone number by heart, and only call the number printed on the back of your card, never a number from a text message. Number nine. Your safe deposit box is not insured.

Everybody thinks what's in the box is protected like the money in the account. It isn't. The government deposit insurance covers deposits, your checking, your savings, your CDs, up to the limit. It does not cover the contents of a safe deposit box. If there's a fire, a flood, or a theft, and it does happen, you're relying on whatever the bank's agreement says, and that's often very little, or on your own homeowner's insurance. And when the box rent goes unpaid, or when the owner passes away and nobody knows about it, the bank can eventually drill it and send the contents to the state as unclaimed property.

So, three things. Keep a list and photos of what's in the box, and keep that list at home. Check whether your homeowner's or renter's policy covers items in the box. And make sure somebody you trust knows the box exists, and is named on it the right way.
Number ten. Forgotten money doesn't stay at the bank.

This is... This is the quietest one. If an... If an account has no activity for a few years, no deposits, no withdrawals, no contact from you, the bank marks it dormant. Uh... The good news: it's not lost. Every state has an unclaimed property office, and searching your name is free. Never pay a company to do it for you. This is the last one and it's the most important. Scammers today call you pretending to be your bank's fraud department. Your caller ID even says the bank's name. They know your name.
